Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
(1) The worst and longest economic crisis in the modern industrial world, the Great Depression in the United States had devastating consequences for American society. At its lowest depth (1932–33), more than 16 million people were unemployed, more than 5,000 banks had closed, and over 85,000 businesses had failed. Millions of Americans lost their jobs, their savings, and even their homes. The homeless built shacks for temporary shelter—these emerging shantytowns were nicknamed Hoovervilles; a bitter homage to President Herbert Hoover, who refused to give government assistance to the jobless. The effects of the Depression—severe unemployment rates and a sharp drop in the production and sales of goods—could also be felt abroad, where many European nations still struggled to recover from World War I.

(2) Although the stock market crash of 1929 marked the onset of the depression, it was not the cause of it: Deep, underlying fissures already existed in the economy of the Roaring Twenties. For example, the tariff and war-debt policies after World War I contributed to the instability of the banking system. American banks made loans to European countries following World War I. However, the United States kept high tariffs on goods imported from other nations. These policies worked against one another. If other countries could not sell goods in the United States, they could not make enough money to pay back their loans or to buy American goods. (3) And while the United States seemed to be enjoying a prosperous period in the 1920s, the wealth was not evenly distributed. Businesses made gains in productivity, but only one segment of the population—the wealthy—reaped large profits. Workers received only a small share of the wealth they helped produce. At the same time, Americans spent more than they earned. Advertising encouraged Americans to buy cars, radios, and household appliances instead of saving or purchasing only what they could afford. Easy credit policies allowed consumers to borrow money and accumulate debt. Investors also wildly speculated on the stock market, often borrowing money on credit to buy shares of a company. Stocks increased beyond their worth, but investors were willing to pay inflated prices because they believed stocks would continue to rise. This bubble burst in the fall of 1929, when investors lost confidence that stock prices would keep rising. As investors sold off stocks, the market spiraled downward. The stock market crash affected the economy in the same way that a stressful event can affect the human body, lowering its resistance to infection.

(4) The ensuing depression led to the election of President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1932. Roosevelt introduced relief measures that would revive the economy and bring needed relief to Americans suffering the effects of the depression. In his 100 days in office, Roosevelt and Congress passed major legislation that saved banks from closing and regained public confidence. These measures, called the New Deal, included the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which paid farmers to slow their production in order to stabilize food prices; the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insured bank deposits if banks failed; and the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulated the stock market. Although the New Deal offered relief, it did not end the Depression. The economy sagged until the nation entered World War II. However, the New Deal changed the relationship between government and American citizens, by expanding the role of the central government in regulating the economy and creating social assistance programs.

AnswerA: federally sponsored housing programs.

AnswerD: the effectiveness of the Hoover administration in dealing with the crisis.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
In the following passage, the narrator reflects upon his early days in Australia. I discovered that soap operas were excellent learning aids: their plots universal and repetitive, the histrionic acting transpicuous^1; I could concentrate on the colloquial dialogues. I watched the cast of Sons and Daughters squabble and The Young Doctors flirt with the nubile nurses. I sat in front of the TV and repeated the dialogue line by line. I copied the rhythm, the idioms and the tone. I discovered that to learn to speak is to learn to listen.

I couldn't formulate sentences quickly enough to converse at normal speed, so I took to planning for a conversation like for a game of chess; the first 'hello' was the opening gambit. I anticipated all the possible responses from my opponent and devised my replies accordingly. Preparing such a script gave me the semblance of a spontaneous speaker in common situations like asking for directions or ordering fast food. But I was still utterly useless when talking to girls, who always came up with startling lines that reduced me to a stammering idiot. When I did finally think of a witty response, it was usually hours after they had left.

No English teacher in Hong Kong had ever mentioned the prosodic characteristics of the language. It has its own distinctive pitch, melody, tempo and tones. Even meaningful noises, like a grunt for admiration or contempt, are all different in English and Chinese.

Curiously, dozing in a busy shopping mall helped me to tune in to this. In the nevernever land between wakefulness and sleep, vowels and consonants receded while the musical quality of English became prominent; its intonations tintinnabulated like glass bells, its distinct rhythm became a drumbeat I could clap to. My relationship with English became a lot friendlier once I started to learn not just grammar and vocabulary, but also to listen to its music.

1. Transpicuous: an uncommonly used word that means transparent, clear, or easy to understand.

ComprehensionText:
The Case Against the Campfire
Ask most Australians to picture a perfect camping trip and they will describe a crackling fire under the stars. I understand the appeal. I grew up toasting marshmallows over glowing coals. But after many years of camping, I have come to believe that the campfire is a habit we should be ready to give up. A small gas stove does the job better, and it leaves the bush in better shape.
The first problem is risk. A campfire can seem tame, but it takes only one strong gust of wind to carry a burning ember into dry grass. Even after the flames die down, coals can stay hot for many hours. People who cover them with sand or soil often believe they have put the fire out, when they have simply hidden the heat. Fire authorities advise drowning coals with water until they are cold to the touch, yet many campers skip this step when they pack up in a hurry. Every year, rangers find fires still smouldering at sites that campers left that morning.
The second problem is less obvious. Fallen branches and logs are not just untidy leftovers on the forest floor. They are homes. Beetles, spiders, skinks and small marsupials shelter in and under them, while fungi slowly break them down, returning goodness to the soil. When campers gather armfuls of dead wood near a popular campsite, year after year, the ground around it becomes bare. The creatures that relied on that timber must move on or disappear. This is why many national parks now ban the collection of firewood altogether.
A stove avoids both problems. It lights in seconds, boils water quickly and can be switched off completely with a twist of the wrist. It works on rainy evenings when every stick is soaked, and it can be packed away cold within minutes of dinner. There is no smoke in your eyes, and no jumper that smells like a chimney for days afterwards.
I learnt this lesson from my uncle Ray. For twenty years he was a volunteer with the Rural Fire Service, and he spent many summer nights on the fire line. On our family camping trips, my cousins begged him for a bonfire. He never lit one. Instead, he would smile, set up his battered blue stove and put the kettle on. At the time I thought he was simply being boring. Now I think I understand.
I am not asking anyone to give up the joy of camping. The stars still shine, stories can still be told, and hot chocolate tastes just as good from a stove. Next time you head into the bush, try leaving the firewood behind. You may find you miss the fire far less than you expected.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
The Weaver Who Lit the Sky
Long ago, in a village near the top of the world, winter was a time of endless dark. For two whole months the sun did not rise at all, and the people lived by the glow of their fires and the cold light of the stars. The old ones said that the North Wind sometimes walked among people in disguise, testing whether their hearts were warm or cold.
In that village lived a young weaver named Ylva. Her cloth was the finest for many days' travel, because of her colours. Every summer, while the sun circled the sky day and night, she wandered the hills gathering flowers, berries, lichen and roots. She boiled them in great pots to make her dyes: crimson from cranberries, gold from birch leaves, deep green from moss and a violet that no one else could match. She dipped her wool in them and hung the skeins to dry in the long summer light. Each thread was a summer she had saved.
That year, Ylva wove a cloak from her brightest threads. It shimmered like the sea at sunset, and she meant to wear it to the midwinter gathering, where every eye would turn to her.
Three nights before the gathering, there was a knock at her door. Outside stood a gaunt old man in a grey coat. His beard was white with frost, and when he spoke, his breath turned to ice crystals even in the warmth of her doorway.
'I have travelled far, and the dark has worn me thin,' he said. 'Do you have a scrap of colour to spare?'
Ylva hesitated. Her baskets of thread were nearly empty. All that remained of her summer was the cloak. She thought of the gathering and of everyone admiring her. Then she looked at the old man's tired face, and at the darkness pressing against the windows, and she took the cloak from its hook and placed it in his hands.
He smiled for the first time. 'Generous hearts are rare,' he said, 'rarer than violet dye.' Then he turned and walked into the night. Ylva watched him go. Strangely, though fresh snow covered the path, he left no footprints, and the cloak in his arms rippled and flapped although the air was perfectly still.
On the night of the gathering, the villagers stepped outside and gasped. Across the black sky rippled great curtains of light, green and violet, crimson and gold, folding and unfolding like cloth shaken out in a strong wind. The whole village stood in the snow with faces lifted, glowing with colour.
Ylva did not wear a fine cloak that night. But she stood among her neighbours with her head tipped back, and she knew every one of those colours by name.
To this day, people in the far north say that when the lights dance, the weaver's cloak is being shaken out across the sky, so that no one need face the long dark without a little summer.

AnswerD: tall

Living Pantries
In the red sand country of central Australia, rain can stay away for months. Plants wilt, flowers vanish and food for small creatures becomes scarce. Yet deep beneath the mulga scrub, colonies of honeypot ants have a clever way to survive the lean times. They store their food inside the bodies of their own sisters.
Like all ants, honeypot ants live in colonies with a queen and thousands of female workers. Some workers forage above ground. They collect sweet nectar from flowers and honeydew, a sugary liquid produced by tiny sap-sucking insects that feed on mulga trees. But instead of storing this food in wax cells, as bees do, the ants feed it to a special group of workers called repletes.
A replete's job is simply to eat and to wait. Foragers pass liquid into its mouth again and again until its abdomen stretches to many times its normal size. A fully loaded replete can be as large as a grape, its body so swollen that the thin skin between its hard plates becomes almost see-through and glows amber, like a drop of honey. Too heavy to walk, the repletes hang from the ceilings of chambers that may lie more than a metre below the surface, where the soil stays cool and damp.
There they remain, sometimes for months. When the season turns dry and foragers return empty-handed, hungry workers stroke a replete's head with their antennae. In response, it brings up a droplet of stored food and passes it mouth to mouth. In this way a few hundred living storage jars can keep an entire colony alive until the rains return. Scientists believe the repletes may store water as well, which would be just as precious in the desert.
This arrangement is not without risk. A replete cannot run from danger, and a burst replete is food lost for good. The deep, narrow tunnels help protect them, and guard ants patrol the entrances.
Honeypot ants are also important to people. For thousands of years, Aboriginal people of the desert regions have dug for them as a sweet bush food. Finding a nest takes skill: a digger must recognise the small entrance hole, then follow the tunnel down through hard ground, sometimes for a metre or more. The reward is a cluster of golden repletes, which are eaten by biting off the sweet abdomen. Traditionally, diggers leave part of the nest alone so that the colony can recover.
Honeypot ants show that survival does not always depend on being fast, strong or fierce. Sometimes it depends on planning ahead and sharing. A honeypot nest is small, quiet and easy to overlook, yet each one holds a carefully guarded store of sweetness that can last through months of drought.
